Generate all hashes.note: Runs every digest this build can compute; the list is the DecodeBox set, not CyberChef’s.

Parse TLV.note: Parse TLV; keys and values are hex strings, not byte arrays

Show Base64 offsets.note: Show Base64 offsets; a text report rather than highlighted HTML

Encode text.note: Encode text; the platform's ~38 WHATWG code pages, so no EBCDIC or IBM DOS pages

Decode text.note: Decode text; the platform's ~38 WHATWG code pages, so no EBCDIC or IBM DOS pages

Escape string.note: Escape string; hand-written escaping rather than jsesc, same options

Fuzzy Match.note: Fuzzy Match; ranked text lines rather than highlighted HTML

Offset checker.note: Offset checker; a marker line rather than highlighted HTML

Diff.note: Diff; `+`/`-` markers rather than `<ins>`/`<del>`, and no CSS or JSON modes

Sleep.note: Sleep; capped at 3 seconds so it cannot outlive the step timeout

Parse colour code.note: Parse colour code; every notation as text, without the colour picker

JavaScript Beautify.note: JavaScript Beautify; brace-driven re-indent, no quote normalisation

JavaScript Minify.note: JavaScript Minify; whitespace and comments only, not terser's renaming

Render Markdown.note: Render Markdown; emits escaped HTML as text rather than rendering it

JPath expression.note: JPath expression; paths, indexes, slices and recursive descent, but not filter expressions

Parse X.509 certificate.note: Parse X.509 certificate; a text report, with the common extensions decoded by name

Protobuf Decode.note: Protobuf Decode; schema-less, so fields are reported by number and wire type

Protobuf Encode.note: Protobuf Encode; takes the field list Protobuf Decode produces, not a .proto schema

HTTP request.wont: Sends the input to a server the recipe names. Recipes are shareable by URL, so this would turn a shared link into an exfiltration channel — and DecodeBox promises that nothing leaves the browser.

DNS over HTTPS.wont: Same reason as HTTP request: it would send the input to a third-party resolver, which the tool's privacy promise rules out.

Translate DateTime Format.note: Translate DateTime Format; moment-style tokens on the platform's own time-zone data

Template.note: Template; a Mustache subset, with no helpers or partials, so a recipe cannot run code

XPath expression.note: XPath expression; paths, //, @attr, text() and simple predicates — no axes, functions or unions

Jsonata Query.wont: A complete query language of its own, several thousand lines to implement faithfully. JPath expression covers path queries over JSON.

Zip.note: Zip; one entry per archive, stored or deflated, without password encryption

JWT Sign.note: JWT Sign; HS, RS and ES families, with PEM keys for the asymmetric ones

JWT Verify.note: JWT Verify; refuses alg:none rather than reporting an unsigned token as valid

Bcrypt.note: Bcrypt; cost capped at 16 so a mistyped setting cannot hang the tab

Avro to JSON.note: Container files with the null or deflate codec; snappy, bzip2, xz and zstandard are named and refused.

YAML to JSON.note: A documented subset: block and flow syntax, block scalars, multiple documents. Anchors, aliases and tags are refused rather than guessed at.

Typex.note: The mechanism, with the rotor wirings supplied as an argument. Typex wirings were never published the way Enigma’s were, and shipping an unverifiable set would look authoritative while being wrong.

Extract Audio Metadata.note: MP3 (ID3v1 and ID3v2), FLAC, Ogg Vorbis, WAV and AVI.

Automated Validation Test Op.wont: It exists to exercise CyberChef’s own test harness, not to transform anything. DecodeBox’s test suite does that job.

Show on map.wont: It fetches map tiles from a third-party server, which would send the coordinates you are analysing off the machine. Nothing in DecodeBox leaves the browser.

Bzip2 Compress.note: Written here rather than taken from a library; verified by handing its output to libbz2.

LZMA Decompress.note: The plain .lzma container. Streams inside .xz or .7z need unpacking first.

LZMA Compress.note: A bounded greedy match finder rather than an optimal parser: the output is valid LZMA and a little larger than 7-Zip’s.

XPRESS LZ77+Huffman Decompress.note: The format records no decompressed size, so without the optional size argument a few bytes of padding can follow the data.

Invert Image.note: Reads PNG and BMP; JPEG and GIF are named and refused rather than guessed at.

Rotate Image.note: Quarter turns. An arbitrary angle would need resampling that invents pixels.

Convert Image Format.note: PNG and BMP. Writing JPEG would need an encoder that throws information away, which is the wrong default for evidence.

Split Colour Channels.note: One picture with the three channels side by side, rather than a zip of three files.

RSA Encrypt.note: OAEP. Textbook RSA with no padding is not offered, because it is not encryption.

RSA Sign.note: PKCS#1 v1.5 and PSS, through Web Crypto.

ECDSA Sign.note: P-256, P-384 and P-521, in raw or DER form.

P-list Viewer.note: Binary and XML, read to the same JSON either way.

Convert co-ordinate format.note: Decimal degrees, degrees minutes seconds, degrees decimal minutes and geohash. UTM, MGRS and OSNG are projections onto an ellipsoid rather than another spelling, and are not included.

Scatter chart.note: Drawn as a PNG rather than SVG: the output pane will not render SVG, because SVG is markup that can carry script.

Add Text To Image.note: A built-in 5x7 bitmap font. Measuring a web font needs a canvas, which the image code deliberately avoids.

SSDEEP.note: Tridgell’s spamsum algorithm with the published constants. There is no libfuzzy on the build machine to check interoperability against, so a comparison against a hash from ssdeep itself is unconfirmed; comparisons between two DecodeBox hashes are exact.

CTPH.note: The same algorithm as SSDEEP, under its generic name.

Lorenz.note: The machine, with the wheel patterns supplied as an argument: the pins changed monthly and there is no single set to ship.

Colossus.note: The 1+2 break-in count Colossus was built to run, over the chi 1 and chi 2 start positions. The switch panel of the real machine is not simulated.

YARA Rules.note: Text, hex and regex strings with the nocase, wide, ascii and fullword modifiers; conditions with counts, at, filesize, the uint family and the counting forms. Modules (pe, elf, math, hash) and for-loops are named and refused rather than ignored.

BLAKE3.note: Hash, keyed hash and key derivation, with extendable output. Checked against the published vectors either side of the 1 KiB chunk boundary and up to 4 KiB, which is what exercises the tree.

Ascon Hash.note: Ascon v1.2, the version selected by the lightweight cryptography process. NIST SP 800-232 changes the initial values, so a 2025 library will not agree.

Ascon Encrypt.note: Ascon-128 v1.2, checked against the first entry of the known-answer set.

Parse PGP Key.note: Packet structure, algorithms, user IDs, subkeys, signatures and version-4 fingerprints. Checked against GnuPG’s own output for an RSA key and an Ed25519 key with a subkey.

GOST Encrypt.note: The S-boxes are an argument: the standard leaves them as a parameter, different organisations were issued different sets, and shipping one under a name that might not be the set a message was written with would be worse than asking.

GOST Key Wrap.note: The RFC 4357 wrap: ECB over the key, bound by GOST’s own MAC over the UKM.

Disassemble x86.note: A disassembler is a table of every encoding the architecture defines, and one wrong entry turns a report into a wrong answer that reads like a right one. Not attempted rather than attempted badly.

Disassemble ARM.note: The same reason as Disassemble x86: an instruction table that cannot be verified offline is not worth shipping.

GOST Hash.note: GOST R 34.11-94 is defined by a large substitution parameter set that cannot be derived and was not available offline. A guessed constant produces a digest that is confidently wrong.

Streebog.note: GOST R 34.11-2012 needs a 256-byte substitution, a 64x64 binary matrix and twelve 64-byte round constants, none of them derivable and none available offline.

MD6.note: No published vector was available offline to check an implementation against, and a hash nobody can check is a hash that should not be shipped.

Snefru.note: Its S-boxes are eight kilobytes of values drawn from a random source in 1990. They cannot be derived and were not available offline.

SIGABA.note: The cipher rotors are stepped by the control and index banks through a wiring whose details could not be reproduced with confidence offline. A rotor machine that steps wrongly produces ciphertext no real machine could.

LS47 Encrypt.note: The marker and padding rules could not be reproduced from the specification offline, and ciphertext from a near-miss would not decrypt anywhere else.

Generate PGP Key Pair.note: OpenPGP key generation needs the whole standard: string-to-key, the packet layer, and public key algorithms Web Crypto does not provide. Parse PGP Key reads a key that already exists, which is what most analysis needs.

PGP Encrypt.note: The OpenPGP message layer needs session keys, its own CFB variant, compression and several algorithms the platform does not carry.

PGP Verify.note: See PGP Encrypt. A partial verifier is the worst case of all: it would report success for messages it had not really checked.

SM2 Encrypt.note: SM2 is elliptic curve arithmetic over a curve Web Crypto does not carry, so it would have to be written out by hand — the one thing this project refuses to do with public key cryptography.

Generate QR Code.note: Reed-Solomon coding, masking and a format-information BCH. Left until it can be checked against a real decoder, which was not available offline.

Parse QR Code.note: Finding and rectifying a symbol in a photograph, then decoding it. See Generate QR Code.

Optical Character Recognition.note: Needs a trained OCR engine. Shipping a model would be a dependency larger than the rest of the tool.

Render PDF.note: A PDF renderer is a project rather than an operation. Detect File Type and the text extractors read what is inside one.

Play Media.note: The output pane renders pictures and text. Playing audio would mean handing untrusted bytes to a media decoder inside the page, which is a larger attack surface than the feature is worth.

JavaScript Parser.note: A JavaScript parser is a language implementation. JavaScript Beautify and JavaScript Minify cover what people reach for it for.

Jq.note: A query language of its own, like Jsonata. JPath expression covers path queries.

Syntax highlighter.wont: It emits HTML for a pane that renders it. DecodeBox’s output pane renders text and pictures and never HTML, deliberately: building markup out of untrusted input is the bug class the whole tool exists to avoid.

GOST Sign.note: GOST R 34.10 signatures are elliptic curve arithmetic over curves Web Crypto does not carry, and would have to be written out by hand — the one thing this project refuses to do with public key cryptography. The same reason as SM2.
